item.title: Short Point Lists for CNFs and Stronger Constant-Depth Circuit Hardness
item.description: arXiv:2610.27127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a short-description decomposition of bounded-width CNFs. For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, every width-$b$ CNF on $m$ variables is an exact disjoint union of at most $2^{\varepsilon m}$ width-$b$ CNFs, each determined by $2^{O_\varepsilon(b)}\log(m+1)$ satisfying assignments. For every fixed $d\ge3$, we prove a worst-case size lower bound of $2^{\Omega_d((n\log n)^{1/(d-1)})}$ against depth-at-most-$d$ unbounded-fan-in AND/OR circuits with input negations for three polynomial-time Boolean families: inverse trace over binary fields, the Goldreich--Tal trilinear function, and OpenAI's polynomial evaluator with its original parameters. All parameter bits count as inputs. For inverse trace, every such circuit of size at most $S$, where $n\le S\le2^{c_dn^{1/(d-1)}}$, has uniform sign correlation at most $2^{-\eta_dn\log\log S/(\log S)^{d-1}}$. Here $c_d,\eta_d>0$ depend only on $d$. This improves on the classical parity correlation bound. The lower bounds combine the decomposition with restriction arguments; the correlation bound additionally uses common partial decision trees. We also construct exact nonuniform AND/OR circuits for inverse trace of size $2^{O(n^{2/3})}$ at depth eight and $2^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}$ at depth nine. For every fixed integer $h\ge2$, the construction gives depth-$(4h+1)$ circuits of size $2^{O_h(n^{1/h}\log n)}$. The upper bounds implement finite-field evaluation and interpolation using circuits that enumerate intermediate states.
item.dc:creator: Xin Li, Yan Zhong

item.title: On the Support Geometry and Complexity of LABS
item.description: arXiv:2610.27329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LABS are a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem arising in sequence design and statistical physics, yet the formal complexity of the standard fixed-geometry problem remains unresolved. We study how zero-energy complexity changes when support geometry is included as part of the input and then progressively restricted. For unary standard LABS, we establish membership in $\NP$ and a sparsity/Mahaney consequence: Karp NP-hardness would imply $\Ptime=\NP$. For Pair-Set-LABS and Masked-LABS, zero-energy feasibility is polynomial-time decidable when every pair group or masked row has at most three terms and is NP-complete when four terms are allowed. NP-completeness persists when active supports are restricted to contiguous intervals.
item.dc:creator: William Cruz-Santos

item.title: Space Complexity of Reachability in Simple Path Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.27879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One of the central questions in space complexity is whether nondeterministic logspace computations ($\textsf{NL}$) can be simulated in unambiguous logspace ($\textsf{UL}$). A stronger notion, \emph{reach unambiguity} ($\textsf{RUL} \subseteq \textsf{UL} \cap \textsf{co}\textsf{UL}$), requires every configuration reachable from the start to have exactly one computation path (Buntrock et.al. 91). While directed graph reachability is $\textsf{NL}$-complete, planar graph reachability is in $\textsf{UL}$ and undirected graph reachability is in deterministic logspace ($\textsf{L}$). In this work, we study the space complexity of reachability problem for restricted directed graph families and show the following. - For reach unambiguous graphs (graphs with at most one path from start vertex to every vertex), Lange (Lange 97) showed that reachability is in $\textsf{RUL}$. As our main result, we show that for simple path graphs (introduced in Kannan et.al. 08), which contains reach unambiguous graphs), where each vertex has at most one simple path from the start, we show that the reachability problem lies in $\textsf{UL} \cap \textsf{co}\textsf{UL}$. - Our first result can also be equivalently stated as: the recognition problem for simple path is in $\textsf{UL} \cap \textsf{co}\textsf{UL}$ if and only if the reachability problem restricted to simple path graphs is also in $\textsf{UL} \cap \textsf{co}\textsf{UL}$. Inspired by this, we investigate the complexity of graph recognition versus graph reachability for graph classes. Observe that for any graph class, solving reachability (for the class) also solves the recognition problem for that class. We show that for reach unambiguous graphs, solving recognition is as hard as solving reachability (making both of them $\textsf{RUL}$-complete). (Abstract shortened to meet arXiv limits)
item.dc:creator: Krishnamoorthy Dinesh, Chandana Sasidharan

item.title: Lower Bounds for Minimal-Transversal Enumeration of Bounded-Dimension Hypergraphs and the maximum Minimal Hitting Set Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.28012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present lower bounds for the maximum minimal hitting set problem and for the problem of enumeration of minimal transversals in bounded-dimension hypergraphs. Our starting point is the recent reduction of Kobayashi, Kurita, and Wasa (2026), developed to establish ETH-based hardness of hypergraph dualization. Adapting their construction, we show that, under ETH, deciding whether a hypergraph $\mathcal{G}$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ hyperedges has a minimal transversal of size at least $k$ cannot be done in time $n^{f(k)}m^{o(k)}$, for an arbitrary computable $f$. We transfer this bound to the following decision problem: given a dimension-at-most-$r$ hypergraph and a family of $s$ of its minimal transversals, decide whether another exists. Under ETH, this problem admits no uniform algorithm with running time $n^{f(r)}(s+1)^{o(r)}$. Under SETH, for every fixed $t \geq 2$, it admits no algorithm with running time $\poly(|\mathcal{G}|)(s+1)^c$ for dimension at most $2t$ and any $c<t$. As corollaries, the same exponent obstructions hold for the total time of any output-polynomial enumeration algorithm, with $s$ replaced by the total number of minimal transversals. In particular, polynomial delay is excluded under SETH already for dimension at most four.
item.dc:creator: Arnaud Mary

item.title: Singular Linear Differential-Algebraic Equations with Constant Coefficients Necessarily Admit Non-Computable Solutions
item.description: arXiv:2610.28188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: If a regular linear differential-algebraic equation has a unique solution, this solution is known to be Turing computable. In contrast, this paper shows that singular linear differential-algebraic equations exhibit fundamentally different computability properties. More precisely, we show that for every linear differential-algebraic equation (LDAE) with constant computable coefficients, there exists a computable input function with strong regularity properties such that the LDAE admits a unique solution, yet this solution is not Turing computable. In fact, the solution is non-computable at certain computable times.
item.dc:creator: Holger Boche, Volker Pohl, H. Vincent Poor, Frank H. P. Fitzek

item.title: Two $\operatorname{ReLU}$ Layers is All You Need
item.description: arXiv:2610.28587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that every $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network can be exactly simulated by a $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network with two hidden layers. We present two proofs: one that is based on fillings in homological algebra and a direct combinatorial proof.
item.dc:creator: Florestan Brunck, Christoph Hertrich, Kilian Ruess, Jack Stade, Amir Yehudayoff

item.title: Matrix Multiplication from Polynomial Packings: A Constructive and Elementary Proof of $\omega\le9/4$
item.description: arXiv:2610.28627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a self-contained constructive proof that the matrix multiplication exponent satisfies $\omega\le9/4$. This bound was recently claimed by OpenAI~\cite{original} through non-constructive arguments in Strassen's asymptotic spectral framework, counting exact scalar arithmetic operations over the complex numbers. We explicitly construct a Strassen-style matrix multiplication identity and obtain the bound by ordinary block recursion. For every $\gamma>0$, the resulting algorithm multiplies two $n\times n$ integer matrices using $O(n^{9/4+\gamma})$ integer arithmetic operations.
item.dc:creator: Rafael Pass

item.title: Partitionability is NP-complete
item.description: arXiv:2610.27083v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that the problem of deciding whether a simplicial complex is partitionable is NP-complete in dimensions two and higher, answering a 1995 question of Kleinschmidt and Onn.
item.dc:creator: Russ Woodroofe

item.title: A Short Note on Algorithms For The Noisy $k$-XOR Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.27147v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This mostly expository note studies the sample-noise regimes in which the testing problem for noisy $k$-XOR in dimension $n$ can be efficiently solved. Concretely, we ask what pairs $(\beta, \delta)$ admit algorithms running in time $n^{O(k)}$ where $m = n^\beta, \beta \in [0,k]$ is the number of samples and $\mathsf{Bern}(n^{-\delta}),\delta \in (0,+\infty)$ is the noise distribution. The current state-of-the-art algorithms are: I. A folklore algorithm when $\beta > 1, \delta>1$ based on Gaussian elimination; II. A folklore algorithm when $\beta\ge k/2$ based on the birthday paradox; III. A recent algorithm in the regime $\beta > \delta + k(1-\delta), \delta \in (0,1)$ based on a reduction to the first algorithm [DJ24,CSZ24]. IV. Extending [AF09], we strictly improve the last regime to $\beta > \delta + (k-1)(1-\delta), \delta \in (0,1).$ These algorithms correspond to efficiently finding short cycles in uniform hypergraphs and can be equivalently phrased as algorithmic Moore bounds.
item.dc:creator: Kiril Bangachev

item.title: Deterministic Shift Equivalence Testing for Sparse Polynomials
item.description: arXiv:2610.27168v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the shift equivalence testing problem for high-degree sparse multivariate polynomials. Given explicit spar se representations of two polynomials $f,g\in\mathbb{Q}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, with exponents encoded in binary, sparsities $s$ and $t$, and total degree at most $d$, the task is to decide whether there is a vector $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{Q}^n$ such that $f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{a})\equiv g(\mathbf{x})$. Furthermore, one needs to output such a vector if it exists. Dvir, Oliveira, and Shpilka (ICALP 2014) studied shift equivalence for low-degree arithmetic circuits. Their framew ork does not apply directly to sparse polynomials, which are not closed under shifts, and they left open whether shift equivalence of sparse polynomials admits an efficient deterministic algorithm. We answer this question positively over $\mathbb{Q}$. If the input coefficients have bit-size at most $\tau$, we sh ow that a rational shift of polynomial bit-size exists whenever the polynomials are shift equivalent. Moreover, our alg orithm outputs such a shift and has a running time of $\operatorname{poly}(n,s,t,\tau,\log d)$ in the bit model. The ar ithmetic and structural parts of our result also hold over any field of characteristic zero or characteristic larger th an $d$.
item.dc:creator: Markus Bl\"aser, Pranjal Dutta, Sagnik Dutta, Gorav Jindal

item.title: Small sums of roots of unity: polylogarithmic exceptional sets and conditional separation
item.description: arXiv:2610.27231v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove a polylogarithmic exceptional-set estimate for symmetric five-term sums of roots of unity of arbitrary order. More precisely, at most $O((\log(2N))^{11})$ points of the $N$-grid satisfy $|1+2\cos(2\pi x)+2\cos(2\pi y)|<\exp(-C(\log(2N))^{13})$. This implies the corresponding bound for small conjugates at the reduced conductor: outside polylogarithmically many real embeddings, every such sum is at least quasipolynomially large. The proof is unconditional and combines a polynomial-vector-field multiplicity estimate, arithmetic jet determinants, analytic propagation, and interpolation determinants for nearby grid points. As a companion result, assuming a uniform number-field $abc$ conjecture, we prove that every sum of a fixed number of distinct prime-order roots of unity has modulus at least $\exp(-\varepsilon p)$ for every $\varepsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large primes $p$, uniformly in the exponents. That proof uses simultaneous compression of the exponents, discriminant estimates, and cyclic resultants.
item.dc:creator: Qi Cheng

item.title: Simple Strategy-Iteration with Dantzig's Rule is not Strongly Polynomial on Turn-Based Deterministic Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.27386v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study turn-based deterministic zero-sum games with discounted and long-run average costs. For discounted costs, we establish exponential and superpolynomial iteration lower bounds for the simple strategy-iteration method with Dantzig's rule under unrestricted costs and unit weights, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this shows for the first time that the method is not strongly polynomial even when all action costs belong to $\{-1,0,1\}$. For long-run average costs, we establish an exponential iteration lower bound for termination of a Dantzig counterpart with unrestricted costs and prove that it admits a strongly polynomial implementation with unit weights.
item.dc:creator: Sanyou Mei

item.title: A 55-Addition Rank-23 Scheme for $3\times3$ Matrix Multiplication via Exact Two-Sided Minimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.27451v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a scheme that multiplies two $3\times3$ matrices with 23 multiplications and 55 additions over any ring, one addition below the previous record of 56 (Sun, 2026) and the first below 56 for exact non-commutative $3\times3$ multiplication without a change of basis. The scheme forms 13 signed combinations of the entries of A and 14 of B, takes 23 products, and recombines them with 28 further additions; its correctness is machine-checked in Lean 4. The previous records, from 60 down to 56, were obtained by greedy common-subexpression elimination, which only bounds each side of a scheme from above. We minimize both input sides exactly by chain covering, and the output side exactly through the transposition principle: the 9-by-23 output map costs its transpose plus 14, and the transpose is a 9-input map that the input-side minimizer solves exactly. Applied to Perminov's cn122 scheme (class i19w225c4efh, published at 58 additions) this gives 55 = 13 + 14 + 28, where greedy elimination reaches only 29 on the output side. The same method shows that Sun's representative is output-optimal at 56, and an exact orbit-wide computation over the Heule-Kauers-Seidl database shows that the record class is the only database class attaining 55.
item.dc:creator: Greg Sidebottom

item.title: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
item.description: arXiv:2610.28141v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.
item.dc:creator: Ioannis Anagnostides, Constantinos Daskalakis, Gabriele Farina, Noah Golowich, Tuomas Sandholm, Brian Hu Zhang

item.title: Subjective Valuations Make It Hard to be Fair: The Complexity of Resource Allocation to Groups of Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.28213v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the parameterized complexity of finding an EF1 allocation of indivisible items in the group-sharing setting, which has received increasing attention in recent years. There, items are not allocated to individual agents but rather to one of two (or possibly more) groups, and agents within that group all share the assigned items. We consider both the "fixed" (EF1-Fix) and "variable" (EF1-Var) group cases, where in the former the assignments of agents to groups are prescribed. While both are NP-hard in the classical sense, we show that their algorithmic behavior differs significantly from the parameterized perspective. As our main results, we: (1) prove that both cases are NP-hard even when the number of agents is a small constant; (2) circumvent this hardness by establishing fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Var w.r.t. the number of "subjective" items, that is, items which are viewed as chores or goods by different agents---but rule out an analogous result for EF1-Fix; and (3) establish fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Fix w.r.t. the number of item types, but link the existence of an analogous fixed-parameter algorithm for EF1-Var to a fundamental open question in the setting of Integer Linear Programming.
item.dc:creator: Argyrios Deligkas, Eduard Eiben, Robert Ganian, Tiger-Lily Goldsmith, Marlene Gr\"undel, Simon Wietheger

item.title: Hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ over finite chain rings
item.description: arXiv:2610.28368v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a bounded-error quantum polynomial-time algorithm for finding hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ over any effectively presented finite chain ring $R$. We call auxiliary group elements or subgroups used to extract information through oracle queries \emph{probes}. For chain length at least two, elementary abelian socle probes first recover the complete flag modulo the maximal ideal. When the residue field has size $q\ge3$, we reconstruct the flag recursively, lifting rank-one terminal members one digit at a time. The intermediate digits reduce to abelian hidden subgroup problems, while the final digit is a finite-field multiple-shift problem solved using learning from subset and Fourier sampling. For $q=2$, where distinct flags can have the same stabilizer, we instead lift the conjugate parabolic subgroup through the congruence filtration. A final linear system determines it modulo normalizer directions. The algorithm outputs generators with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log|R|,\log(1/\epsilon))$. Consequences include $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ for every $N\ge2$ and, with an explicit maximal-order presentation, $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal{O_K}/N\mathcal{O_K})$ for number fields $K$.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Imran

item.title: Exact Envy-Free Cake Cutting with Polynomial Expected Queries
item.description: arXiv:2610.28535v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Envy-free cake cutting asks how to divide a resource so that no agent prefers another agent's share. Finding such a division with few queries about preferences has been a longstanding challenge. Aziz and Mackenzie gave the first query bound depending only on the number $n$ of agents: a tower of six $n$'s. Subsequent improvements culminated in Ye and Bai's single-exponential bound of $n^{O(1)}2^n$. A large gap remains between this deterministic upper bound and Procaccia's general lower bound of $\Omega(n^2)$. Whether polynomially many queries suffice is a central open question in fair division. We show that a polynomial expected query bound is possible. Our randomised protocol uses only independent, uniformly sampled points from the cake as its source of randomness. For every profile of $n$ agents with nonnegative, additive, nonatomic valuations, the protocol has the following guarantees: (1) It terminates with probability one. (2) Every allocation it returns is complete and exactly envy-free. (3) Its expected number of Robertson-Webb queries is $\widetilde{O}(n^{30})$. The expectation is taken solely over the protocol's random choices, with no distributional assumptions on preferences.
item.dc:creator: Simon Mackenzie, Mashbat Suzuki

item.title: Separating Circuits: Switching Lemmas and Random Restrictions
item.description: arXiv:2109.13917v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Non-uniform circuit complexity classifies Boolean functions by the size and depth of the gate networks required to compute them. Because $\mathsf{P} \subseteq \mathsf{P/poly}$, proving super-polynomial circuit lower bounds for $\mathsf{NP}$ problems offers a combinatorial route toward separating $\mathsf{P}$ from $\mathsf{NP}$, formalized by the Karp-Lipton theorem ($\mathsf{NP} \subseteq \mathsf{P/poly} \implies \mathsf{PH} = \Sigma_2^p$). While general circuit lower bounds for explicit functions in $\mathsf{NP}$ remain linear, exponential lower bounds hold for bounded-depth circuits via random restrictions and polynomial approximations. We give a self-contained treatment of both paradigms and their consequences. First, we establish Shannon's counting lower bound, Lupanov's $(1+o(1))2^n/n$ synthesis upper bound, and the Karp-Lipton theorem via SAT self-reducibility. Second, we prove H{\aa}stad's Switching Lemma via Razborov's canonical decision-tree encoding, showing that a $k$-CNF or $k$-DNF under a $p$-random restriction collapses to decision-tree depth less than $s$ except with probability at most $(5pk)^s$, and derive the optimal $2^{\Omega(n^{1/(d-1)})}$ lower bound (and matching $O(n 2^{n^{1/(d-1)}})$ upper bound) for Parity in depth-$d$ $\mathsf{AC}^0$. Third, we present the Razborov-Smolensky method over $\mathbb{F}_p$, proving that $\mathrm{MOD}_q \notin \mathsf{AC}^0[p]$ for distinct primes $p \neq q$ and establishing a $2^{\Omega(n^{1/(2d)})}$ lower bound for Parity against $\mathsf{AC}^0[3]$. Finally, we examine structured restrictions for $k$-Clique and average-case depth hierarchies, four consequences of the Switching Lemma -- oracle separations of $\mathsf{PH}$ from $\mathsf{PSPACE}$, Linial-Mansour-Nisan Fourier concentration, Nisan-Wigderson pseudorandom generators, and $\mathsf{AC}^0$-SAT algorithms -- and the Razborov-Rudich Natural Proofs barrier.
item.dc:creator: Bruce Changlong Xu

item.title: Classifying Approximation Algorithms: Understanding the APX Complexity Class
item.description: arXiv:2111.01551v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many NP-hard optimization problems that are equivalent under Karp reductions behave very differently when we ask for polynomial-time approximations. This paper studies the complexity class APX, a subclass of NPO consisting of optimization problems that admit polynomial-time algorithms with constant-factor approximation guarantees. We first review the formal structure of NPO, define L-reductions and PTAS-reductions, and prove that L-reductions preserve polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS). Using the Probabilistically Checkable Proofs (PCP) theorem as a starting point, we present self-contained L-reductions establishing the APX-completeness of Max-3SAT, Max-2SAT, Max-NAE-3SAT, and Max-Cut, and we situate APX within the broader hierarchy FPTAS, PTAS, APX, logAPX, and polyAPX. We then examine structural consequences of the polynomial hierarchy for self-improvability and APX-intermediate problems such as Min-Bin-Packing, and review how APX-hardness arises in Bayesian optimal mechanism design for three-bidder single-item auctions. Turning to algorithm design, we analyze three core techniques across the APX and logAPX boundary: linear programming relaxation with Raghavan-Thompson randomized rounding for multicommodity congestion minimization, Goemans-Williamson semidefinite programming rounding for Max-Cut, and greedy, dual-fitting, and randomized rounding methods for Min-Set-Cover. We close by discussing bounded-query approximation oracles and recent constant-factor and sub-3/2 advances on the asymmetric and metric traveling salesman problems.
item.dc:creator: Bruce Changlong Xu, Arthur Lee

item.title: Fine-Grained $\mathsf{AC}^0$ Lower Bounds for $k$-OV, $k$-XOR, and $k$-SUM via Colored Subgraph Isomorphism
item.description: arXiv:2608.08578v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the circuit cost of selecting $k$ objects satisfying orthogonality, zero XOR, or modular zero SUM. Our main lower bounds in nonuniform $\mathsf{AC}^0$ use a common framework of depth-zero projections from colored subgraph isomorphism. The projections use dimension, row count, or bit width $O(k\log n)$ and preserve circuit size, depth, and gate orientation. OV inputs satisfy pairwise distinctness within each array. Our direct XOR bounds require odd $k$, while SUM admits both parities. Stronger lower bounds for suitable source patterns transfer through the same framework to all three targets. For every fixed depth $d$ and sufficiently large fixed $k$, we prove unconditional lower bounds $n^{\Omega(k)}$ for OV and $(n/k)^{\Omega(k)}$ for XOR and SUM, with an absolute constant in the exponent independent of $d$ and $k$; only the threshold on $n$ may depend on $(d,k)$. For $k\to\infty$ with $k=n^{o(1)}$, combining our projections with Beame's small-clique lower bound yields $n^{\Omega_d(\min\{\sqrt{k},\log n\})}$ at every fixed depth $d$. We strengthen the exponent to $\Omega(k)$ at depth two in both orientations and at depth three with a top disjunction. The depth-three result allows unrestricted bottom fan-in and literal polarity; its proof bounds the probability that a planted copy forms a minterm of an arbitrary fixed CNF over a random background.
item.dc:creator: Haoxing Lin

item.title: Metric Dimension is NP-complete on Graphs of Treewidth Two
item.description: arXiv:2610.21133v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The metric dimension of a connected graph is the least number of vertices whose distance vectors distinguish all vertices. We show that deciding whether the metric dimension of a graph is at most a given integer is NP-complete on graphs of treewidth at most two, and even on two-connected two-terminal series-parallel graphs of pathwidth at most five. As the problem is polynomial on trees, the graphs of treewidth one, this settles the treewidth threshold of its hardness, which was known to lie between two and twenty-four. The reduction is from satisfiability of formulas in which every literal occurs at most twice. To such a formula with $n$ clauses and $r$ variables it associates a two-terminal series-parallel graph $G_\varphi$ with $O((n+r)^2)$ vertices and pathwidth at most five, whose metric dimension is $2(n+r)+7$ if the formula is satisfiable and $2(n+r)+8$ otherwise.
item.dc:creator: Tristan Benoit

item.title: Persistent (Co)Homology in Matrix Multiplication Time
item.description: arXiv:2412.02591v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Most algorithms for computing persistent homology do so by tracking cycles that represent homology classes. There are many choices of such cycles, and specific choices have found different uses in applications. Although it is known that persistence diagrams can be computed in matrix multiplication time [8] for the more general case of zigzag persistent homology, it is not clear how to extract cycle representatives, especially if specific representatives are desired. In this paper, we provide the same matrix multiplication bound for computing representatives for the two choices common in applications in the case of ordinary persistent (co)homology. We first provide a fast version of the reduction algorithm, which is simpler than the algorithm in [8], but returns a different set of representatives than the standard algorithm [6] We then give a fast version of a different variant called the row algorithm [4], which returns the same representatives as the standard algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Dmitriy Morozov, Primoz Skraba

item.title: On the hardness of approximating minimum distances of quantum codes
item.description: arXiv:2509.21469v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The problem of computing distances of error-correcting codes is fundamental in both the classical and quantum settings. While hardness for the classical version of these problems has been known for some time (in both the exact and approximate settings), it was only recently that Kapshikar and Kundu showed the hardness of these problems for non-degenerate quantum codes. As our first main result, we get a direct reduction to CSS codes, the most commonly used type of quantum code, from the minimum distance problem for classical linear codes. In particular, our proof uses arguably simpler constructions based on hypergraph product codes. Our second set of results considers the distance of a graph state, which is a key parameter for quantum codes obtained via the codeword stabilized formalism. We show that it is NP-hard to compute/approximate the distance of a graph state, which is a degenerate quantum code, when the adjacency matrix of the graph is the input. This establishes hardness for even degenerate quantum codes, which was not known before. Furthermore, we show this is true even if we only consider X-type errors of a graph state. Our techniques, moreover, imply an interesting classical consequence: the hardness of computing or approximating the distance of classical codes with rate equal to 1/2. One of the main motivations of the present work is a question raised by Kapshikar and Kundu concerning the NP-hardness of approximation when there is an additive error proportional to a quantum code's length. We show that no such hardness can hold for hypergraph product codes. These observations suggest the possibility of a new kind of square root barrier.
item.dc:creator: Elena Grigorescu, Vatsal Jha, Eric Samperton

item.title: Graph-Theoretic Analysis of Phase Optimization Complexity in Variational Wave Functions for Heisenberg Antiferromagnets
item.description: arXiv:2602.04943v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the computational complexity of learning the ground state phase structure of Heisenberg antiferromagnets. Representing Hilbert space as a weighted graph, the variational energy defines a weighted XY model that, for $\mathbb{Z}_2$ phases, reduces to a classical antiferromagnetic Ising model on that graph. For fixed amplitudes, reconstructing the signs of the ground state wavefunction thus reduces to a weighted Max-Cut instance. This links sign optimization of wavefunctions directly to combinatorial optimization.
item.dc:creator: Mahmud Ashraf Shamim, Md Moshiur Rahman Raj, Mohamed Hibat-Allah, Paulo T Araujo

item.title: Detection Is Harder Than Estimation in Certain Regimes: Inference for Moment and Cumulant Tensors
item.description: arXiv:2603.26029v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study estimation and detection of high-order cumulant tensors from $n$ i.i.d. observations of a $p$-dimensional random vector, with performance measured in the tensor spectral norm. Under sub-Gaussianity, we show that the minimax rate for estimating the order-$d$ cumulant tensor is $\sqrt{p/n}\wedge 1$. In contrast to covariance estimation, the natural plug-in estimator obtained by replacing population moments in the moment--cumulant formula with sample moments, which we call the sample cumulant tensor, is generally not rate-optimal for $d\ge 3$, and we construct an estimator that attains the minimax rate. On the computational side, we study testing whether the $d$-th order cumulant tensor vanishes after whitening. We provide evidence, under a model-specific low-degree conjecture, that detection is computationally hard when $n\ll p^{d/2}$. At the same time, we identify a regime in which an efficiently computable estimator achieves error smaller than the separation at which polynomial-time tests can reliably distinguish the null from the alternative under the same conjecture. This reveals an unusual reverse detection--estimation gap: computationally efficient detection can be harder than computationally efficient estimation. The underlying reason is that the relevant loss, tensor spectral norm, is itself NP-hard to compute, creating a new form of computational--statistical gap.
item.dc:creator: Runshi Tang, Yuefeng Han, Anru R. Zhang

item.title: The Low-Individual-Degree Test Without the Diagonal-Lines Test Is Not Quantum-Sound
item.description: arXiv:2609.12346v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: To prove the quantum soundness of the classical low-individual-degree test, the authors of \cite{JNVWY20LID} defined three subtests, namely the axis-parallel lines test, the self-consistency test, and the diagonal-lines test. An interesting question is whether the diagonal-lines test can be removed. In this paper, we show that the diagonal-lines test cannot simply be removed without another compatibility mechanism. Consequently, replacing the "conditional linear functions" by "coordinate deletion functions" in the proof of MIP*=RE, as mentioned in \cite{JNVWY20LID}, does not by itself preserve the required soundness. The authors of \cite{JNVWY20LID} found an example that requires the diagonal-lines test when \((m, d, q) = (2, 2, 4)\); we give an example when \((m, d) = (2, 2)\) and \(q\) is any odd prime.
item.dc:creator: Honghao Fu, Nengkun Yu, Tianrun Zhao

item.title: Quantum Soundness of a Total-Degree Line-versus-Point Test
item.description: arXiv:2609.27129v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove quantum soundness of the total-degree diagonal line-vs-point test using the individual-degree soundness theorem of Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright, and Yuen. A random change of coordinates yields projective polynomial decoders of total degree at most $md$. The uniform-line slice of the test bounds the weight of outcomes of degree greater than $d$, which are removed by a common relabeling. This reduction does not yield a dimension-independent soundness bound: the $\operatorname{poly}(m)$ dependence of the individual-degree theorem persists, as discussed in Section 1.2 of arXiv:2009.12982.
item.dc:creator: Honghao Fu, Nengkun Yu, Tianrun Zhao

item.title: The rank of 3x3 matrix multiplication over F2 is 23
item.description: arXiv:2610.11823v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rank of the tensor of $3\times 3$ matrix multiplication over the field with two elements is at most $23$ by Laderman's algorithm, and Rudich and Rousseau recently proved that it is at least $22$. We prove that it equals $23$. Hence Laderman's algorithm uses the fewest multiplications among all bilinear algorithms over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and among all bilinear algorithms with integer coefficients. The proof uses the substitution method in the form developed by D'Ambrosio, Wang and Yang et al., which bounds the number of first factors of a decomposition that lie in a given subspace of the space of first factors. We sharpen these bounds for $111$ of Wang's $496$ classes of subspaces, constrain the ranks of the first factors through a $27\times 27$ flattening of the tensor, and list, up to symmetry, all sets of $22$ first factors that satisfy these constraints. An exact completion search shows that none of them is the set of first factors of a decomposition. The computation emits certificates, which are checked in the Lean 4 proof assistant. In one formal proof the largest checks are evaluated as compiled code, and in a second one the kernel evaluates every check, so that its final theorem depends only on the three standard axioms of Lean. The Lean proofs build on the formalization of Rudich and Rousseau and import their table of bounds and their reduction for block algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Tejasvi Singh Tomar
